processes: Absorbing water and minerals from the soil
Anchoring the plant in the ground
Transporting water up to the stem
plainLanguageExplanation: A root is the part of a plant that grows down into the soil. It does three big jobs: it anchors the plant so it doesn't blow away or get pulled out, it soaks up water and minerals from the soil, and it sometimes stores food. The very tip of the root has a protective cap that pushes through the soil. Just behind the tip, tiny finger-like hairs called root hairs grow out and greatly increase the surface area, which lets the root absorb a lot of water. From the root, that water is carried up into the stem and then to the leaves.

keyFacts.label: Direction
keyFacts.value: Roots grow downward into the soil (gravitropism)

keyFacts.label: Main jobs
keyFacts.value: Anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, store food

keyFacts.label: Absorption surface
keyFacts.value: Root hairs - millions of tiny extensions that boost surface area

keyFacts.label: Root cap
keyFacts.value: A protective covering at the very tip that shields it while pushing through soil

keyFacts.label: No chloroplasts
keyFacts.value: Roots live in dark soil so they do not photosynthesize; leaves do that

keyFacts.label: Food storage
keyFacts.value: Many roots store sugar and starch (like carrots and potatoes)

whyItMatters: Roots are the underground engine of every plant. Without them plants could not stand, could not get water, and could not survive. Understanding roots explains why plants can survive storms, why watering matters, and how crops store food underground in things like carrots.
tagline: The plant's underground anchor and drinking straw
didYouKnow: One large plant may have millions of root hairs, giving it a huge surface area to soak up water from the soil.
